title: NCMHCE Practice Exam 1
note: Questions and the key for items 1-48 are from the published excerpt. The key for items 49-132 was drafted 2026-10-04 and needs clinical review before launch.

cases.name: Marcus
cases.diagnosis: Major depressive disorder, recurrent episode, moderate (F33.1)

cases.name: Tyler
cases.diagnosis: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, moderate (F31.12)

cases.name: Luis
cases.diagnosis: Schizophrenia, first episode, currently in acute episode (F20.9)

cases.name: Hannah
cases.diagnosis: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, with good or fair insight (F42.2)

cases.name: Walter
cases.diagnosis: Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.23)

items.question: Which information is MOST important for the counselor to gather during this first session?

options.A: His relationship with his late father and how he grieved that loss
options.B: Current suicidal thoughts and access to lethal means
options.C: His wife's view of the marriage and how she thinks he is coping
options.D: A detailed history of his employment, injury, and the circumstances of the layoff

items.rationale: Depression with hopelessness, recent job loss, and a middle-aged male profile all raise suicide risk. Risk and access to lethal means must be assessed in the first session, before other history.

whyNot.A: May matter clinically, but safety comes first.
whyNot.C: Collateral view is secondary to direct risk assessment.
whyNot.D: Useful later, but not a safety priority.

items.question: Which detail BEST supports the 'recurrent' specifier?

options.A: His current symptoms have lasted about three months
options.B: He has lost weight without trying to
options.C: The layoff happened several weeks before his symptoms began
options.D: A prior episode at 30, followed by years of feeling like himself

items.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires at least two episodes separated by at least two consecutive months without meeting criteria for a major depressive episode. His episode at 30, followed by years of feeling like himself, meets that standard.

whyNot.A: Duration describes the current episode, not recurrence.

items.question: Marcus says, “I'm only here because my wife made me.” Which response is MOST therapeutic?

options.A: “Coming here wasn't your idea, and you're not sure what this can offer you.”
options.B: “Counseling only works if you want to be here, so let's talk about that.”
options.C: “Your wife must be very worried about you to push you to come in.”
options.D: “A lot of men feel that way at first, but most find it helps once they give it a chance.”

items.rationale: A reflection that accepts his reluctance lowers defensiveness and builds the alliance. It communicates respect for his autonomy without arguing or making promises.

whyNot.B: Sounds like a condition or a threat.
whyNot.C: Shifts focus to his wife rather than to him.

items.question: Marcus asks whether his employer's disability insurer will see what he says. What should the counselor do?

options.A: Tell him insurers automatically receive the full record when a claim is filed
options.B: Postpone the question until he has signed all the necessary release forms
options.C: Explain what he can authorize and the legal limits of confidentiality
options.D: Assure him that nothing he says will ever leave the counseling room

items.rationale: Informed consent includes an honest explanation of confidentiality and its limits. That covers what can be released with his authorization and the exceptions required by law.

whyNot.B: Consent questions should be answered at the start.

items.question: After Marcus's answer to PHQ-9 item 9, what should the counselor do NEXT?

options.A: Arrange immediate inpatient hospitalization because he endorsed the item
options.B: Readminister the PHQ-9 at the next session to see if the answer changes
options.C: Refer him to a psychiatrist for an antidepressant evaluation before going further
options.D: Ask directly about ideation, plan, intent, and past attempts

items.rationale: A positive item 9 calls for an immediate, direct risk assessment, such as the C-SSRS. That assessment determines the level of risk and the response.

whyNot.A: Not indicated before risk is assessed.
whyNot.C: May help later but doesn't address current risk.

items.question: The assessment shows passive ideation with no plan or intent and several protective factors. Which intervention is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Recommend voluntary inpatient admission until his mood has stabilized
options.B: Build a written safety plan with him that addresses the rifles
options.C: Have him sign a no-harm contract agreeing to call the clinic before acting on any thoughts
options.D: Schedule follow-up only if he reports that the ideation has increased

items.rationale: Safety planning with lethal-means counseling is an evidence-based practice for passive ideation. Reducing access to firearms is one of the most effective prevention steps.

whyNot.A: Too restrictive for this risk level.
whyNot.C: No-suicide contracts lack evidence and can create false security.

items.question: Marcus says his family would be better off with the insurance money. Which response BEST reflects his experience?

options.A: “Let's focus for a minute on the things that are still going well.”
options.B: “Part of you has started to believe you're a burden to your family.”
options.C: “Have you thought about how your sons would feel if something happened?”
options.D: “That isn't true. Your family needs you, not the insurance money.”

items.rationale: Reflecting perceived burdensomeness shows understanding and opens discussion of a key suicide risk factor. The other responses argue, induce guilt, or change the subject.

whyNot.A: Premature shift away from risk content.
whyNot.D: Arguing invalidates him and ends exploration.

items.question: Marcus says that in his family you don't tell strangers your business. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Move on to a CBT thought record so the session time is used efficiently
options.B: Explain the research showing that counseling is effective for depression
options.C: Explore his family and cultural beliefs about seeking help
options.D: Gently suggest that this belief may be a form of denial about his depression

items.rationale: Broaching cultural and family beliefs about help-seeking shows respect and builds trust. It also helps the counselor fit treatment to his worldview.

items.question: Which treatment goal is written MOST appropriately?

options.A: Marcus will stop thinking about suicide and feeling like a burden to his family
options.B: Marcus will feel less depressed and more like himself by the end of treatment
options.C: Marcus will complete two scheduled activities per week for four weeks, recorded on a log
options.D: Marcus will understand where his depression comes from and why it returned

items.rationale: log Goals should be specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART). This one names a behavior, a frequency, a timeframe, and a way to measure it.

whyNot.A: Not a realistic or measurable short-term goal.

items.question: Marcus says the activity worksheets are pointless. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Remind him that progress in counseling depends on completing assignments
options.B: Switch to a different treatment model that doesn't use homework
options.C: Explore what got in the way and adapt the task together so it fits him
options.D: Re-explain why homework is an important part of behavioral activation

items.rationale: Collaboratively troubleshooting barriers keeps him engaged and treats nonadherence as information. Adapting the format, for example tracking on his phone, can respect his style.

whyNot.A: Places blame and risks the alliance.

items.question: Marcus wants his pastor involved in his care. What should the counselor do?

options.A: Discourage the pastor's involvement to keep treatment strictly clinical
options.B: Obtain a signed release and coordinate with the pastor as a support
options.C: Call the pastor directly to let him know about the suicide risk
options.D: Suggest he rely on the pastor for support instead of continuing counseling

items.rationale: With written consent, natural supports such as clergy can strengthen safety and engagement. Faith is also a protective factor he has named.

items.question: Marcus's wife calls asking whether he still has suicidal thoughts. There is no release. How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Tell her about the ideation, since his safety is involved
options.B: Share the details, since as his spouse she is part of his support system
options.C: Confirm that he is a client but decline to share anything else
options.D: Share nothing without his authorization, but listen to what she wants to report

items.rationale: Without a release, confidentiality applies even to a spouse. The counselor can receive information from her without disclosing anything, and can encourage Marcus to sign a release.

whyNot.A: No imminent danger here justifies a disclosure.
whyNot.C: Confirming client status is itself a disclosure.

items.question: Which feature BEST separates Priya's presentation from typical academic stress?

options.A: Worry that eases quickly once a friend or parent reassures her
options.B: Trouble falling asleep during high-pressure weeks like midterms and finals
options.C: Worry that is mostly focused on her upcoming exams and grades
options.D: Hard-to-control worry about many areas, most days, for over six months

items.rationale: GAD requires excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple domains, more days than not, for six months or more, with associated symptoms. Her eight-month pattern across many areas fits.

whyNot.A: Reassurance-responsive worry isn't typical of GAD.
whyNot.C: A single focus suggests situational stress.

items.question: Which step is MOST important to rule out another explanation for her symptoms?

options.A: Assess caffeine and substance use and recommend a medical evaluation
options.B: Explore childhood experiences in depth to find the origin of her worry
options.C: Refer her for ADHD testing, since she struggles to keep up with work
options.D: Give her a personality inventory to identify traits linked to anxiety

items.rationale: GAD can only be diagnosed if symptoms aren't better explained by a substance or a medical condition. High caffeine intake and possible thyroid issues must be ruled out.

whyNot.C: Nothing in the case suggests ADHD.
whyNot.D: Not indicated to rule out other causes.

items.question: Priya apologizes again for wasting the counselor's time. Which response is MOST helpful?

options.A: “You're worried about being a burden, even here.”
options.B: “You're not wasting my time at all. This is exactly what I'm here for.”
options.C: “Let's move on and talk about the goals you have for counseling.”
options.D: “Why do you feel like you're wasting my time?”

items.rationale: Reflecting the feeling beneath the apology validates her and shows how her worry plays out in the room. Reassurance and “why” questions tend to cut exploration short.

whyNot.B: Reassurance can feed the worry cycle.

items.question: When should the counselor tell Priya about the center's eight-session limit?

options.A: During informed consent in the first session, with referral options
options.B: Only if she asks about how many sessions she can have
options.C: Not at all, because it could add to her anxiety about treatment
options.D: In session seven, when the limit becomes relevant to planning

items.rationale: Informed consent includes the length, limits, and continuity of services. Telling her early lets her make informed choices and avoids abandonment later.

whyNot.B: Consent is the counselor's job to cover.

items.question: How should Priya's GAD-7 score of 15 be interpreted?

options.A: Mild range
options.B: Minimal range
options.C: Moderate range
options.D: Severe range

items.rationale: GAD-7 cutoffs are 5 (mild), 10 (moderate), and 15 (severe). A score of 15 falls at the start of the severe range and gives a baseline for tracking progress.

items.question: Priya says she can't disappoint her parents. Which approach is MOST culturally responsive?

options.A: Encourage her to set firm boundaries with her parents about her career
options.B: Invite her parents to the next session to discuss their expectations
options.C: Explore what family obligation means to her, on her terms
options.D: Help her see that her career is ultimately her own decision to make

items.rationale: Understanding collectivist values and family sacrifice from her perspective avoids framing interdependence as a problem. It helps her find solutions that fit her values.

whyNot.B: Premature and made without her input.

items.question: Which approach has the STRONGEST evidence for treating Priya's GAD?

options.A: Cognitive behavioral therapy targeting worry and intolerance of uncertainty
options.B: Psychoanalytic exploration of early conflicts that may underlie the worry
options.C: EMDR processing of the distressing memories connected to her anxiety
options.D: Nondirective supportive listening that allows her to set the pace

items.rationale: CBT, including cognitive restructuring, applied relaxation, and work on intolerance of uncertainty, is a first-line psychotherapy for GAD.

items.question: Priya is considering taking her roommate's Adderall. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Explore the pros and cons with her and share information about the risks
options.B: Treat it as unrelated to her anxiety and return to the worry work
options.C: Report the roommate to campus police for distributing a controlled substance
options.D: Tell her it's illegal to take someone else's prescription and she must not

items.rationale: A motivational interviewing stance respects her autonomy and supports an informed choice. Stimulants can also worsen anxiety, palpitations, and sleep.

whyNot.C: Not a mandated report and would harm trust.

items.question: Priya says she failed at worry time. Which response is MOST helpful?

options.A: “Everyone struggles at first, so don't be so hard on yourself.”
options.B: “You noticed the worry showing up. What made it hard to set it aside?”
options.C: “Then worry time probably isn't the right technique for you.”
options.D: “It may be that you didn't give it a full try yet.”

items.rationale: Reframing the attempt as useful data and exploring barriers counters her perfectionism. It also keeps the skill in play.

items.question: What is the main purpose of the worry-time technique?

options.A: To gradually get rid of worry completely by the end of treatment
options.B: To share her worries with a trusted friend at a set time each day
options.C: To postpone worry to a set time, building a sense of control
options.D: To uncover the childhood origins of her worry during the set time

items.rationale: Stimulus control of worry teaches that worry can be postponed and contained. That weakens the belief that worry is uncontrollable.

whyNot.B: That's reassurance-seeking, which can maintain worry.

items.question: Priya's father calls again demanding to know if she attends. How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Neither confirm nor deny her attendance without her written consent
options.B: Confirm her attendance, since he is paying her tuition
options.C: Tell him she's doing well so that he stops calling the center
options.D: Share records, since FERPA gives parents access to student records

items.rationale: Priya is an adult, and her counseling records are confidential. Paying tuition gives her father no right to information. Counseling records are generally treated as treatment records, not ordinary education records.

whyNot.B: Payment doesn't create a right to information.
whyNot.D: Misreads how counseling records are protected.

items.question: Which goal fits Priya's request within the session limit?

options.A: Resolve the family conflict about her career path before finals
options.B: Lower her GAD-7 score below 10 within five weeks using worry-management skills
options.C: Complete a full course of long-term treatment at the counseling center
options.D: Eliminate all of her anxiety before finals begin in five weeks

items.rationale: The goal is specific, measurable, and achievable within brief treatment and her five-week timeframe.

whyNot.A: Outside the brief-treatment scope for now.

items.question: Danielle takes long detours to avoid highways. Which PTSD symptom cluster does this represent?

options.A: Alterations in arousal and reactivity
options.B: Intrusion
options.C: Avoidance
options.D: Negative alterations in cognition and mood

items.rationale: Avoiding external reminders such as places, activities, or situations is Criterion C (avoidance) in DSM-5-TR.

whyNot.B: Intrusion includes memories, nightmares, and flashbacks.

items.question: Which step is MOST appropriate regarding her nightly drinking?

options.A: Diagnose alcohol use disorder at intake based on her nightly use
options.B: Treat the drinking as understandable self-medication for her nightmares
options.C: Screen her alcohol use with a standardized tool such as the AUDIT
options.D: Tell her she must stop drinking before trauma therapy can begin

items.rationale: Co-occurring alcohol use is common in PTSD. Standardized screening guides whether further assessment and integrated care are needed.

items.question: Danielle says the counselor, as a civilian, can't understand. Which response BEST builds the alliance?

options.A: “Trauma is trauma, whatever the source, and the healing process is the same.”
options.B: “I've worked with a lot of veterans, so I have a good sense of military life.”
options.C: “Let's not focus on our differences. What matters is that you're here.”
options.D: “You're right that I haven't been there. I'd like to understand what it was like.”

items.rationale: Acknowledging the limits of the counselor's experience and inviting her to teach shows humility and respect for military culture.

items.question: The counselor has not been trained in a trauma-focused protocol. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.A: Tell her trauma-focused work isn't necessary for her to improve
options.B: Provide supportive counseling indefinitely until she feels ready
options.C: Get training and supervision, or refer her to a trained provider
options.D: Use the protocol after carefully reading the treatment manual

items.rationale: Counselors must practice within their competence. Trauma-focused protocols require specific training, and treatment decisions should rest on her clinical needs.

items.question: How is Danielle's PCL-5 score of 52 BEST interpreted?

options.A: It confirms the PTSD diagnosis without the need for a clinical interview
options.B: It suggests she may be exaggerating symptoms to support a disability claim
options.C: Consistent with probable PTSD and a baseline for tracking progress
options.D: It falls below the range usually considered clinically significant

items.rationale: The PCL-5 is a screening and monitoring tool. Scores above roughly 31–33 suggest probable PTSD, and change over time tracks treatment response.

items.question: Danielle says, “It should have been me driving.” Which intervention BEST addresses this?

options.A: Begin imaginal exposure to the memory of the attack right away
options.B: Reassure her that the switch was not her fault and no one could have known
options.C: Socratic questioning to examine the evidence about her responsibility
options.D: Interpret the statement as hidden anger toward her friend for switching

items.rationale: In CPT, self-blame is treated as a stuck point, often driven by hindsight bias. Socratic dialogue helps her reach a more balanced view herself.

whyNot.A: Premature and not how CPT handles stuck points.
whyNot.B: Reassurance rarely shifts a stuck point.

items.question: How should the counselor respond to Danielle's report of yelling at her daughter?

options.A: Move on, since yelling at a child is not a form of abuse
options.B: File a child abuse report right away because of the repeated yelling
options.C: Refer the family to family court for a custody evaluation
options.D: Gather more information about the incidents and her daughter's safety

items.rationale: The facts presented don't suggest reportable abuse. Assessing further clarifies safety and opens work on parenting under stress.

whyNot.B: Not supported by what she described.

items.question: Which treatment is MOST supported by evidence for Danielle's PTSD?

options.A: Long-term psychodynamic therapy focused on her earlier relationships
options.B: Relaxation training and sleep hygiene as the main treatment
options.C: A trauma-focused therapy such as CPT or prolonged exposure
options.D: Single-session psychological debriefing about the IED attack

items.rationale: Clinical practice guidelines, including the VA/DoD guidelines, recommend trauma-focused psychotherapies such as CPT, PE, and EMDR as first-line treatment for PTSD.

whyNot.D: Not effective and may cause harm.

items.question: Danielle wants to stop trauma work after missing a session. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Validate her distress, explore the avoidance, and revisit the rationale
options.B: End treatment, since missing a session shows she isn't ready for the work
options.C: Insist that stopping trauma work now would be a serious mistake
options.D: Agree to stop trauma work and switch to relaxation training instead

items.rationale: The urge to avoid, especially after an anniversary, is itself a PTSD symptom. Exploring it while respecting her choice keeps her engaged and informed.

whyNot.D: Colludes with avoidance without exploring it.

items.question: Her AUDIT score is 12. How should treatment be structured?

options.A: Require sobriety for at least 30 days before any trauma work begins
options.B: Address PTSD and alcohol use together in an integrated plan
options.C: Set the alcohol use aside until the PTSD symptoms have improved
options.D: Refer her to an alcohol treatment program first, then resume PTSD work

items.rationale: Integrated treatment of co-occurring PTSD and substance use is recommended. Trauma-focused therapy can proceed alongside work on drinking.

items.question: How should the counselor track Danielle's progress?

options.A: Measure her symptoms only at intake and again at termination
options.B: Rely on her verbal reports of how she is doing each week
options.C: Readminister the PCL-5 at regular intervals during treatment
options.D: Administer the MMPI-2 monthly to monitor her symptom profile

items.rationale: Routine outcome monitoring with the PCL-5 guides treatment decisions and is built into CPT.

items.question: Danielle asks for a letter supporting her disability claim. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Clarify her role and offer a factual summary, with consent
options.B: Write the letter only if she agrees to continue trauma-focused work
options.C: Refuse to provide any records, since treatment is confidential
options.D: Write a letter stating that she is fully disabled by her PTSD

items.rationale: Treating counselors should avoid forensic opinions outside their role. A factual summary with consent is appropriate, and disability determinations belong to independent evaluators.

whyNot.C: She has a right to her records.

items.question: What is the MOST important immediate clinical concern?

options.A: The circumstances of his referral by the peer assistance program
options.B: His withdrawal risk, given his past withdrawal seizure
options.C: His readiness to attend AA and connect with a sponsor
options.D: His family history of alcohol use and his parents' drinking

items.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal can be life-threatening, and a prior seizure raises the risk of another. Medical assessment of withdrawal risk comes first.

items.question: Before sending reports to the peer assistance program, what must the counselor do?

options.A: Wait until the board issues a subpoena for the records
options.B: Send reports, since the board is the source of the referral
options.C: Obtain a written release specifying what is shared, with whom, and why
options.D: Send only a brief summary, since summaries don't require consent

items.rationale: Substance use treatment information requires specific written consent, and federal rules add protections in many programs. Consent must define what is shared, with whom, and why.

whyNot.A: A subpoena isn't the appropriate route here.

items.question: Which instrument measures the severity of alcohol withdrawal?

options.A: CAGE-AID
options.B: AUDIT-C
options.C: BDI-II
options.D: CIWA-Ar

items.rationale: The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, Revised (CIWA-Ar), rates the severity of withdrawal and guides medical management.

items.question: Kevin says he is only here to keep his license. Which response reflects a motivational interviewing stance?

options.A: “You need to admit you're an alcoholic before anything can really change.”
options.B: “Your license matters a lot, and you're not sure yet what needs to change.”
options.C: “Why did you decide to drink before going in to work that day?”
options.D: “If you don't engage in treatment, you'll probably lose your license.”

items.rationale: Reflecting his values and his ambivalence without confrontation reduces resistance and supports change talk.

items.question: Kevin plans to quit cold turkey this weekend. What level of care is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Medically managed withdrawal in an inpatient or residential setting
options.B: A self-guided taper at home with his wife monitoring him
options.C: An intensive outpatient program starting the following week
options.D: Weekly outpatient counseling with a plan to stop over the weekend

items.rationale: Active withdrawal symptoms and a history of withdrawal seizures call for medically monitored or managed withdrawal (ASAM withdrawal management levels).

items.question: Kevin wonders if he could drink only on weekends. Which response is MOST consistent with MI?

options.A: “You should really try AA before deciding anything else.”
options.B: “Controlled drinking doesn't work once someone is dependent on alcohol.”
options.C: “Why weekends? What makes those days different?”
options.D: “You're considering making some change in how you drink.”

items.rationale: Reflecting change talk reinforces his movement toward change. Confronting or directing him at this point would invite resistance.

whyNot.C: Can put him on the defensive.

items.question: Which stage of change BEST describes Kevin's statements in this session?

options.A: Preparation
options.B: Contemplation
options.C: Action
options.D: Precontemplation

items.rationale: He recognizes a problem but is ambivalent about how to change (“maybe I need to do something, but…”). That is contemplation.

whyNot.A: No firm plan has been committed to.

items.question: Kevin says he isn't like the guys at AA. Which response BEST rolls with resistance?

options.A: “AA doesn't feel like a fit. What would you want recovery to look like?”
options.B: “That sounds like your denial talking about how serious this is.”
options.C: “You really need to commit to 90 meetings in 90 days.”
options.D: “You're right that you don't need the same support they do.”

items.rationale: Rolling with resistance accepts his view and invites him to define his own path to support. Mutual-help options besides AA also exist.

items.question: Kevin reports cravings after hard shifts. Which intervention is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Advise him to switch to day shifts to reduce the stress
options.B: Reassure him that cravings will pass on their own with time
options.C: Build a relapse prevention plan for high-risk situations
options.D: Increase sessions to daily until the cravings have eased

items.rationale: Relapse prevention targets his specific triggers, such as post-shift stress, and rehearses coping responses.

whyNot.A: Not a clinical decision for the counselor.

items.question: Kevin asks about medication for cravings. What is the counselor's MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Recommend that he start naltrexone at a standard dose
options.B: Share general information about medications and refer him to a prescriber
options.C: Explain that medications for cravings are only used for opioids
options.D: Discourage medication while he's working on skills in counseling

items.rationale: FDA-approved medications such as naltrexone and acamprosate can help. The counselor gives information and coordinates, and the prescriber decides.

items.question: Kevin's wife asks to join a session. What should the counselor do FIRST?

options.A: Decline, since the treatment contract is for individual counseling
options.B: Meet with her separately first to hear her perspective
options.C: Discuss it with Kevin and get his consent before including her
options.D: Invite her, since she is already involved in Al-Anon

items.rationale: Kevin is the client, so conjoint sessions require his consent. Clear roles and goals should be set before she is included.

items.question: Kevin asks the counselor not to report his relapse. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.A: Keep the relapse confidential, since it was a single night and he's back on track
options.B: Review the signed agreement and discuss how the relapse will be reported
options.C: Report it to the program without discussing it with him first
options.D: End treatment, since the relapse violates his agreement

items.rationale: Kevin signed a release requiring relapse reporting. Transparency preserves trust and honors his informed consent.

whyNot.A: Violates the agreement and misleads the program.
whyNot.D: Relapse isn't a reason to terminate.

items.question: Which feature BEST distinguishes a manic episode from a hypomanic episode in Tyler's case?

options.A: A decreased need for sleep without feeling tired
options.B: Marked impairment, shown by job loss and serious debt
options.C: An elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
options.D: Symptoms that have lasted at least four consecutive days

items.rationale: Mania and hypomania share the same symptom list. What separates them is severity: a manic episode causes marked impairment or needs hospitalization. Losing his job and running up $15,000 in debt is marked impairment.

whyNot.A: Occurs in both mania and hypomania.
whyNot.C: The mood criterion is the same for both.
whyNot.D: Four days is the hypomania threshold; mania needs seven or hospitalization.

items.question: Which action is MOST urgent at intake?

options.A: Teach sleep hygiene strategies to help restore his sleep
options.B: Schedule weekly counseling beginning next week
options.C: Arrange an immediate psychiatric evaluation
options.D: Start CBT for mood regulation during this first session

items.rationale: He has severe sleep loss, grandiose plans, and intends to drive to Las Vegas tonight. Acute mania with impaired judgment needs same-day psychiatric evaluation for safety and medication.

whyNot.A: Sleep hygiene can't treat acute mania.
whyNot.B: A week's delay ignores current risk.
whyNot.D: Insight-based therapy isn't possible during acute mania.

items.question: Tyler speaks rapidly and keeps interrupting. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.A: Match his energy and pace to build rapport quickly
options.B: Confront his grandiose thinking about the app directly
options.C: Use brief, calm, structured statements and set gentle limits
options.D: Let him talk freely without redirecting him

items.rationale: Pressured speech and distractibility respond best to a calm, simple, structured style. Gentle limits keep the session focused without escalating irritability.

whyNot.A: Matching his pace feeds the escalation.
whyNot.B: Confronting grandiosity raises irritability and ruptures rapport.
whyNot.D: Without structure the intake can't be completed.

items.question: Why is the report of his grandfather's “manic depression” clinically relevant?

options.A: It rules out a substance-induced cause for his symptoms
options.B: Bipolar disorder is highly heritable, so it supports the diagnosis
options.C: It shows the illness was learned from family behavior
options.D: It confirms the bipolar diagnosis without further assessment

items.rationale: Bipolar disorder is among the most heritable psychiatric conditions. A first-degree or second-degree relative with it adds weight to the diagnosis, alongside his prior depressive episode.

whyNot.A: Family history doesn't rule out substances; the negative screen does that.
whyNot.D: History supports the diagnosis but never confirms it alone.

items.question: Tyler reports diarrhea and a worsening tremor. What should the counselor do?

options.A: Note the symptoms and review them again at the next session
options.B: Tell him to stop taking lithium right away until he feels better
options.C: Advise him to contact his prescriber today about possible toxicity
options.D: Suggest he drink more water and rest until the stomach bug passes

items.rationale: Diarrhea and dehydration can raise lithium levels, and a worsening tremor is an early sign of toxicity. He needs to contact his prescriber today.

whyNot.A: Possible toxicity can't wait a week.
whyNot.B: Medication changes are the prescriber's call, not the counselor's.
whyNot.D: Fluids alone don't address a possible toxic level.

items.question: Tyler wants to stop lithium because of side effects. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Support stopping the medication, since it is ultimately his choice
options.B: Suggest he switch to an herbal mood supplement with fewer side effects
options.C: Explore his concerns and encourage him to talk with his prescriber first
options.D: Tell him he must stay on the medication to avoid another episode

items.rationale: Side effects are a common reason for stopping lithium, and stopping abruptly raises relapse risk. Exploring his concerns respects his autonomy, and the prescriber can adjust the dose or medication.

whyNot.A: Endorsing an abrupt stop ignores relapse risk.
whyNot.D: A directive response undercuts his autonomy and the alliance.

items.question: Tyler says cannabis helps him sleep. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Refer him to a substance use program right away
options.B: Explore his experience and share how cannabis can affect mood
options.C: Tell him he needs to stop using cannabis immediately
options.D: Agree that it seems to help with sleep and move on to other topics

items.rationale: A nonjudgmental, motivational approach keeps him talking. Cannabis can disrupt mood stability and sleep quality in bipolar disorder, so psychoeducation fits.

whyNot.A: A program referral is premature before assessing his use.
whyNot.C: Demanding abstinence tends to raise resistance.
whyNot.D: Ignoring use misses a real relapse risk.

items.question: Which adjunctive psychosocial intervention is MOST appropriate for Tyler?

options.A: Long-term psychoanalytic therapy
options.B: Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy
options.C: Exposure and response prevention
options.D: Sleep restriction therapy for insomnia

items.rationale: Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy stabilizes daily routines and sleep, which protects against mood episodes. It has evidence as an adjunct to medication in bipolar disorder.

whyNot.A: Not an evidence-based adjunct for bipolar disorder.
whyNot.D: Sleep restriction can trigger mania in bipolar disorder.

items.question: What is the MOST important focus of the family session?

options.A: Decide who is responsible for paying off the recent debt
options.B: Identify early warning signs and build a relapse plan together
options.C: Explore family-of-origin conflict in depth across generations
options.D: Discuss whether Tyler should move out of the family home

items.rationale: Family-focused treatment helps the family recognize early warning signs and agree on a relapse plan. This is the strongest protective step after a manic episode.

whyNot.A: Practical, but not the clinical priority.
whyNot.C: Deep family-of-origin work doesn't fit this stage.
whyNot.D: A living decision isn't the focus now.

items.question: His mother says, “You always ruin everything.” How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Ask Tyler how his mother's comment makes him feel
options.B: Tell her that the comment is emotionally abusive
options.C: Gently interrupt and help her restate her concern as a request
options.D: Let the exchange continue so the pattern can be observed

items.rationale: Critical comments (high expressed emotion) predict relapse in bipolar disorder. Interrupting gently and coaching her to state a specific request models better communication.

whyNot.A: Shifts to Tyler without addressing the pattern.
whyNot.B: Labeling her abusive shames her and breaks the alliance.

items.question: Tyler wants to return to college full time next semester. What should the counselor recommend?

options.A: Leave the decision about college entirely to his mother
options.B: Enroll full time right away to rebuild his confidence
options.C: A gradual return with a lighter course load and accommodations
options.D: Wait at least two years before returning to college

items.rationale: Returning gradually with a lighter load and campus accommodations reduces stress and protects sleep. That lowers relapse risk while supporting his goal.

whyNot.A: The decision is his, made collaboratively.
whyNot.B: A full load right away raises relapse risk.
whyNot.D: An arbitrary two-year wait isn't evidence-based.

items.question: Tyler sends a friend request and offers the counselor a share in his app. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Accept the share, since it has no current monetary value
options.B: Decline both and explain professional boundaries warmly
options.C: Accept the friend request but decline the share in the app
options.D: Ignore both requests without discussing them

items.rationale: Accepting a financial stake or a social media connection creates a dual relationship. Declining warmly and explaining boundaries protects him and the therapy.

whyNot.A: A share is a financial interest regardless of current value.
whyNot.C: A social media connection is also a boundary crossing.
whyNot.D: Ignoring the requests leaves the boundary unclear.

items.question: Which information BEST supports an ADHD diagnosis rather than a situational problem?

options.A: Symptoms at home and school that began before age 12
options.B: He was restless and fidgety during the first session
options.C: His teacher is the one who recommended the evaluation
options.D: He finishes only about half of his classwork each day

items.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires several symptoms before age 12 and in two or more settings. Symptoms at home and school since kindergarten meet both.

whyNot.B: Behavior in one session isn't diagnostic.
whyNot.C: Who referred him doesn't establish the diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Incomplete work has many possible causes.

items.question: Jayden's parents share joint legal custody. What should the counselor do regarding consent?

options.A: Wait until both parents can attend a session together
options.B: Review the custody order and state law on consent
options.C: Rely on the mother's consent, since she brought him in
options.D: Proceed as though the father has no role in decisions

items.rationale: Consent rules for minors with joint legal custody vary by state and by the custody order. The counselor should check both before proceeding.

whyNot.A: Both parents rarely need to attend together.
whyNot.C: One parent's consent may not be enough, depending on the order.
whyNot.D: Joint legal custody usually gives the father decision rights.

items.question: Jayden spins in his chair and asks to play. Which approach BEST builds rapport?

options.A: Insist that he sit still so he learns what sessions are like
options.B: Talk only with his mother while he plays quietly
options.C: Use developmentally appropriate activities that allow movement
options.D: Tell him he'll get a prize at the end if he sits still

items.rationale: Children engage through play and movement. Developmentally appropriate activities build rapport and still allow observation.

whyNot.A: Demanding stillness from a child with ADHD sets up failure.
whyNot.B: Excluding him misses the chance to build rapport.
whyNot.D: A bribe at intake doesn't build a relationship.

items.question: Which assessment is MOST appropriate for gathering symptom information?

options.A: Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory–Adolescent
options.B: Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-V)
options.C: Parent and teacher Vanderbilt rating scales
options.D: Children's Depression Inventory (CDI-2)

items.rationale: Vanderbilt rating scales from a parent and a teacher capture symptoms across settings. That cross-setting picture is what the ADHD diagnosis needs.

whyNot.A: A personality inventory for adolescents, not ADHD symptoms.

items.question: Which step is MOST important before finalizing the diagnosis?

options.A: Rule out vision, hearing, and sleep problems
options.B: Observe him in his classroom for a full school day
options.C: Give a projective drawing test to understand his inner world
options.D: Obtain a full IQ evaluation to assess his learning ability

items.rationale: Vision or hearing problems and sleep-disordered breathing (he snores loudly) can mimic inattention and hyperactivity. They should be ruled out before diagnosing ADHD.

whyNot.B: Helpful but not required to rule out medical causes.
whyNot.D: IQ testing isn't needed to diagnose ADHD.

items.question: Jayden's grandmother says he needs a “good whooping.” Which response is MOST culturally responsive?

options.A: Exclude the grandmother from future family sessions
options.B: Let the comment pass to avoid conflict with the grandmother
options.C: Tell her that spanking is abuse and must stop immediately
options.D: Explore her parenting values respectfully and collaborate

items.rationale: Exploring her values respectfully keeps her engaged as a caregiver. It opens the door to effective, non-physical discipline.

whyNot.A: Excluding her loses a key caregiver.
whyNot.B: Ignoring it leaves harmful discipline unaddressed.
whyNot.C: Labeling and lecturing damages the alliance; reporting depends on actual abuse.

items.question: Which treatment approach is BEST supported for a 9-year-old with ADHD?

options.A: Behavioral parent training plus a medication evaluation
options.B: Weekly child-centered play therapy as the primary treatment
options.C: Waiting to reassess his symptoms in a year
options.D: An elimination diet that removes sugar and additives

items.rationale: For school-age children, guidelines recommend behavioral parent training together with an evaluation for medication.

whyNot.B: Play therapy isn't evidence-based as primary ADHD treatment.
whyNot.C: Waiting a year delays needed treatment.

items.question: Which goal is written MOST appropriately?

options.A: Jayden will complete 80% of classwork in six weeks, per a report card
options.B: Jayden will improve his self-esteem and confidence
options.C: Jayden will stop being disruptive during lessons and transitions
options.D: Jayden will pay better attention in class and at home

items.rationale: A good goal is specific, measurable, and time-limited, and names how progress will be checked.

whyNot.C: States what to stop, not a measurable target.

items.question: Which principle is MOST important for making the token system work?

options.A: Reinforce specific target behaviors immediately and consistently
options.B: Change the target behaviors daily to keep him interested
options.C: Give out all earned tokens at the end of each week
options.D: Take away tokens every time any misbehavior happens

items.rationale: Token systems work when specific target behaviors are reinforced right away and consistently.

whyNot.C: Delayed reward weakens learning for children with ADHD.
whyNot.D: Response cost for every misbehavior turns the system punitive.

items.question: Jayden's father is upset that he wasn't consulted. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Acknowledge his concern and involve him in treatment planning
options.B: Tell him to speak with Jayden's mother about treatment
options.C: Share records only after the mother has agreed to it
options.D: Decline to talk with him until the mother gives permission

items.rationale: A parent with joint legal custody generally has a right to take part in treatment decisions. Acknowledging his concern and involving him, per the custody order, protects the treatment.

whyNot.B: Deflecting to the mother ignores his rights.
whyNot.C: His access doesn't depend on the mother's approval.
whyNot.D: Refusing contact with a legal custodian is inappropriate.

items.question: What is the counselor's MOST appropriate role in the 504 meeting?

options.A: Decide which accommodations the school is required to provide
options.B: With parental consent, share recommendations for accommodations
options.C: Stay out of the meeting, since it's a school matter
options.D: Share the full clinical record with the school team

items.rationale: With parental consent, the counselor can share clinical recommendations to support accommodations. The school team decides what to provide.

whyNot.A: The school, not the counselor, decides accommodations.
whyNot.D: Share only what's needed, with consent.

items.question: Jayden says, “I'm the bad kid in my class.” Which response is MOST therapeutic?

options.A: “You're not bad at all. You're a great kid.”
options.B: “Sounds like you feel people see you as the bad kid.”
options.C: “Who told you that you were the bad kid?”
options.D: “If you follow the class rules, you won't be.”

items.rationale: A reflection of feeling helps him feel understood and opens up how he sees himself.

items.question: What is the MOST urgent priority at this point?

options.A: Develop a meal plan with Emma that she feels comfortable with
options.B: Begin weekly individual therapy to build rapport with Emma
options.C: Explore family dynamics that may be contributing to the restriction
options.D: Coordinate a prompt medical evaluation for medical instability

items.rationale: Rapid weight loss, feeling cold, and heavy exercise point to medical risk. Medical stability must be assessed first in an eating disorder.

whyNot.A: A meal plan comes after medical assessment.
whyNot.B: Rapport matters, but medical risk comes first.
whyNot.C: Family dynamics aren't the urgent priority.

items.question: Which feature is REQUIRED for a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa?

options.A: Recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by guilt
options.B: Loss of menstrual periods for three or more cycles
options.C: A body mass index below 15
options.D: Intense fear of weight gain or behavior blocking gain

items.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, along with restriction and disturbed body image.

whyNot.A: Binge eating describes other disorders or the binge-purge subtype.
whyNot.C: BMI sets severity, not the diagnosis.

items.question: Emma insists she is fine. Which response BEST builds the alliance?

options.A: Acknowledge her perspective with curiosity rather than arguing with her
options.B: Focus on her parents' concerns, since she doesn't see a problem
options.C: Tell her gently that she is in denial about how sick she is
options.D: Show her the weight-loss data to help her see the problem

items.rationale: Curiosity about her view, without arguing, lowers defensiveness and builds the alliance.

whyNot.C: Labeling her as in denial raises resistance.
whyNot.D: Confronting her with data tends to backfire.

items.question: How should the counselor handle confidentiality with Emma and her parents?

options.A: Tell her parents everything she shares in her individual time
options.B: Avoid bringing up confidentiality so she feels comfortable
options.C: Promise Emma that everything she says will stay private
options.D: Explain at the start what stays private and what must be shared

items.rationale: With a minor, the counselor should explain up front what stays private and what must be shared, especially safety concerns.

whyNot.B: Avoiding the topic leads to confusion later.

items.question: Given the pediatrician's findings, what is the MOST appropriate level of care?

options.A: Inpatient medical stabilization
options.B: Nutrition counseling only
options.C: An intensive outpatient program
options.D: Continue weekly outpatient counseling

items.rationale: A resting heart rate of 44 and orthostatic changes signal medical instability. That meets criteria for inpatient medical stabilization.

whyNot.C: Not enough for an unstable patient.
whyNot.D: Not enough for an unstable patient.

items.question: How should the counselor address the coach's “lighter is faster” message?

options.A: Call the coach without telling Emma, since safety is involved
options.B: Advise Emma to quit the team until she has recovered
options.C: Leave it alone, since coaching is outside counseling
options.D: With consent, coordinate with the coach and medical team

items.rationale: With consent, coordinating with the coach and medical team aligns everyone around her health.

whyNot.A: Contacting him without consent breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.B: Quitting may be premature; the team decides on activity limits.
whyNot.C: The coach's message directly affects treatment.

items.question: The counselor feels uneasy because of her own recent dieting. What should she do?

options.A: Seek supervision or consultation to address the countertransference
options.B: Refer Emma to another counselor right away
options.C: Share her own dieting experience with Emma to build connection
options.D: Avoid discussing food in session until the wedding is over

items.rationale: Countertransference around the counselor's own dieting is best handled in supervision or consultation.

whyNot.C: Self-disclosure here serves the counselor, not the client.

items.question: What is the purpose of talking about “the eating disorder” as separate from Emma?

options.A: To reduce blame so the family can fight the illness, not Emma
options.B: To assess whether Emma has a dissociative process
options.C: To avoid directly discussing Emma's eating behavior
options.D: To communicate that Emma isn't responsible for her recovery

items.rationale: Externalizing the illness reduces blame and guilt and unites the family against the disorder. This is a core part of family-based treatment.

whyNot.C: Eating is discussed directly in FBT.
whyNot.D: She stays part of her recovery.

items.question: In phase 1 of family-based treatment, what is the counselor's primary aim?

options.A: Have Emma plan her own meals to build her independence
options.B: Empower the parents to take charge of restoring her weight
options.C: Help Emma gain insight into why she restricts her eating
options.D: Treat the parents' marital conflict that surrounds meals

items.rationale: Phase 1 of family-based treatment puts parents in charge of weight restoration.

items.question: Her father shouts, “Just eat!” How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Coach the parents to use calm, persistent support at meals
options.B: Ask Emma to explain why she won't eat what's served
options.C: Ask the father to leave the session until he can stay calm
options.D: Allow Emma to skip that meal to reduce the conflict

items.rationale: Coaching parents in calm, persistent, nonjudgmental meal support is the FBT approach.

whyNot.C: Removing him loses a key support.

items.question: Emma says everyone would be happier without her. What should the counselor do FIRST?

options.A: Note the comment and continue with the family session
options.B: Reassure her that her family loves her and wants her there
options.C: Tell her parents immediately so they can watch her closely
options.D: Ask her directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, and intent

items.rationale: Any statement suggesting suicidal thinking calls for an immediate, direct risk assessment.

whyNot.C: Assess first, then decide what must be shared.

items.question: Which treatment goal is MOST appropriate at this stage?

options.A: Emma will stop thinking about food and calories during the day
options.B: Emma will like her body and feel comfortable at her new weight
options.C: Emma will eat whatever she chooses without parental involvement
options.D: Restore weight to the range set by her medical team, tracked weekly

items.rationale: Weight restoration to a medically set range, measured weekly, is concrete and fits this stage.

whyNot.C: Removing parental oversight contradicts FBT phase 1.

items.question: Which detail BEST supports schizophrenia rather than schizophreniform disorder?

options.A: The presence of auditory hallucinations commenting on him
options.B: His fixed belief that he is being monitored by neighbors
options.C: Continuous signs of the disturbance for at least six months
options.D: His withdrawal from school and most social contact

items.rationale: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least six months; schizophreniform lasts one to six months. His eight months meets the longer duration.

whyNot.D: Functional decline occurs in both disorders.

items.question: Luis says neighbors watch him through the Wi-Fi. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.A: “That isn't possible. A router can't be used to watch people.”
options.B: “Why do you think the neighbors would want to watch you?”
options.C: “I believe you. Let's figure out how to make them stop.”
options.D: “That sounds frightening, feeling watched in your own home.”

items.rationale: Responding to the emotion, without arguing with or endorsing the delusion, builds trust.

whyNot.A: Arguing with a delusion rarely works and harms rapport.

items.question: Which of Luis's symptoms is a NEGATIVE symptom?

options.A: Belief that neighbors monitor him
options.B: Diminished emotional expression
options.C: Rapid shifts between topics
options.D: Voices commenting on his actions

items.rationale: Diminished emotional expression (flat affect) is a negative symptom.

whyNot.A: A delusion is a positive symptom.
whyNot.C: Disorganized speech is a positive symptom.

items.question: What should happen before the diagnosis is finalized?

options.A: A full neuropsychological battery to measure cognitive decline
options.B: A medical evaluation and substance screening to rule out other causes
options.C: Projective personality testing to understand his thought process
options.D: Interviews with his former professors about his functioning

items.rationale: A first psychotic episode needs a medical workup and substance screening to rule out other causes.

items.question: Luis's mother consulted a curandero. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Tell them spiritual approaches can take the place of medication
options.B: Set it aside as unrelated to Luis's psychiatric treatment
options.C: Advise the family to stop using folk healing during treatment
options.D: Explore the family's beliefs and integrate compatible practices

items.rationale: Respecting cultural healing practices and integrating compatible ones strengthens engagement and adherence.

items.question: Luis dislikes his weight gain. What should the counselor do?

options.A: Suggest he reduce his dose to limit the side effects
options.B: Recommend a strict diet to reverse the weight gain
options.C: Tell him weight gain is a small price to pay for stability
options.D: Encourage him to raise it with his prescriber

items.rationale: Weight gain is a common side effect. The prescriber can adjust or monitor it.

whyNot.A: Dose changes are the prescriber's decision.
whyNot.B: A strict diet isn't the counselor's to prescribe.

items.question: Luis wants to return to work at his uncle's shop. Which approach is MOST evidence-based?

options.A: Individual Placement and Support (IPS) supported employment
options.B: Suggest volunteer work only until he is fully stable
options.C: Wait until all of his symptoms have resolved before working
options.D: Place him in a sheltered workshop to build job skills first

items.rationale: Individual Placement and Support has the strongest evidence for helping people with serious mental illness find competitive work.

whyNot.C: Full remission isn't required to work.
whyNot.D: Sheltered work has weaker outcomes than IPS.

items.question: Luis says he feels stupid for believing the Wi-Fi idea. Which response is MOST therapeutic?

options.A: “Many people feel embarrassed looking back. What's that like for you?”
options.B: “It wasn't stupid at all. You were sick at the time.”
options.C: “Good, that means the medication is really working for you.”
options.D: “Let's not dwell on it and focus on moving forward.”

items.rationale: Normalizing and inviting exploration supports insight without shaming him.

whyNot.C: Focuses on the medication, not him.

items.question: Luis hears voices saying he deserves punishment. What should the counselor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask what the voices tell him to do and whether he'll act
options.B: Contact his parents to let them know about the voices
options.C: Tell him the voices aren't real and can't hurt him
options.D: Increase session frequency to twice a week for now

items.rationale: Command hallucinations about punishment call for an immediate risk assessment: what the voices command and whether he would act on them.

whyNot.B: Assess before deciding what to disclose.

items.question: Which intervention BEST helps Luis cope with distressing voices?

options.A: Encourage him to argue back with the voices when they start
options.B: Interpret the symbolic meaning of what the voices say
options.C: Tell him to ignore the voices until they fade
options.D: CBT for psychosis to examine his beliefs about the voices

items.rationale: CBT for psychosis helps clients examine and change their beliefs about voices, which reduces distress.

whyNot.A: Arguing with voices can raise distress.

items.question: Luis's parents ask about coordinated specialty care. Which description is MOST accurate?

options.A: A medication management clinic run by a psychiatric team
options.B: A residential treatment program for adults with chronic schizophrenia
options.C: Team-based care with therapy, medication, family education, and work support
options.D: A day treatment program for older adults with psychosis

items.rationale: Coordinated specialty care for first-episode psychosis is a team approach: therapy, medication, family education, and supported employment or education.

items.question: Luis's parents ask for updates about the voices. How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Share everything, since they live with him and support him
options.B: Share only what the release allows and suggest a family session
options.C: Refuse to speak with his parents about anything at all
options.D: Share details, since the voices are a safety concern

items.rationale: Share only what the release allows, and offer a family session so he can choose what to share.

whyNot.D: Assess risk first; disclosure must be justified.

items.question: Which feature BEST distinguishes Hannah's obsessions from generalized worry?

options.A: They are intrusive, unwanted, and followed by rituals
options.B: They cause significant distress and interfere with functioning
options.C: They involve everyday concerns like work and health
options.D: They get stronger during stressful periods of life

items.rationale: Obsessions are intrusive and unwanted, and they drive compulsions. Generalized worry is about real-life concerns without rituals.

whyNot.B: Distress and impairment occur in both.

items.question: Which insight specifier fits Hannah's presentation?

options.A: With tic-related features
options.B: With absent insight/delusional beliefs
options.C: With poor insight
options.D: With good or fair insight

items.rationale: She recognizes that her beliefs are probably untrue: "I know it's irrational."

whyNot.B: She doesn't hold the beliefs with delusional conviction.

items.question: Hannah appears ashamed describing her rituals. Which response is MOST helpful?

options.A: Point out that she already knows the fears are irrational
options.B: Reassure her that the rituals don't sound that bad
options.C: Respond with matter-of-fact curiosity and normalize the symptoms
options.D: Move quickly to another topic to ease her discomfort

items.rationale: Matter-of-fact curiosity and normalizing reduce shame and invite disclosure.

items.question: Which instrument BEST measures the severity of Hannah's OCD?

options.A: Mini-Mental State Examination
options.B: Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7
options.C: Beck Anxiety Inventory
options.D: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale

items.rationale: The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale is the standard measure of OCD severity.

items.question: How should Hannah's Y-BOCS score of 26 be interpreted?

options.A: Moderate range
options.B: Severe range
options.C: Extreme range
options.D: Mild range

items.rationale: A Y-BOCS score of 24–31 falls in the severe range.

items.question: Which psychotherapy is FIRST-LINE for Hannah's OCD?

options.A: Psychodynamic therapy
options.B: Exposure and response prevention
options.C: Supportive counseling
options.D: Thought-stopping techniques

items.rationale: Exposure and response prevention is the first-line psychotherapy for OCD.

items.question: How should the counselor address her husband's accommodation?

options.A: Explain how accommodation maintains OCD and plan to reduce it
options.B: Tell him to stop all reassurance and help right away
options.C: Praise him for being so supportive of his wife
options.D: Leave him out of treatment, since Hannah is the client

items.rationale: Family accommodation maintains OCD. Psychoeducation and a gradual plan to reduce it help.

whyNot.B: Stopping abruptly can spike distress and conflict.
whyNot.D: Excluding him misses a key factor.

items.question: Which treatment goal is MOST appropriately written?

options.A: Reduce washing to under 30 minutes a day within 12 weeks
options.B: Hannah will feel less anxious in restaurants and public places
options.C: Hannah will understand why she developed OCD
options.D: Hannah will stop worrying about germs and contamination

items.rationale: Specific, measurable, and time-limited.

items.question: Where should the exposure hierarchy begin?

options.A: An item that causes her no distress at all
options.B: Whatever her husband thinks she can manage
options.C: The most feared situation, so progress happens faster
options.D: An item she rates as moderately distressing

items.rationale: Exposure hierarchies usually begin with a moderately distressing item she can complete.

whyNot.B: Her ratings should guide the order.
whyNot.C: Starting at the top risks dropout.

items.question: Hannah washed her hands five minutes after the exposure. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Tell her the exposure didn't count because she washed afterward
options.B: Stop ERP for now, since she isn't ready to resist rituals
options.C: Review it, praise her effort, and repeat it with ritual prevention
options.D: Let her wash afterward as long as she completes each exposure

items.rationale: Reviewing it, praising her effort, and repeating with response prevention keeps learning on track.

items.question: Hannah asks the counselor to promise it's safe. How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Promise that it's safe to ease her distress in the moment
options.B: Change the subject to her progress this week
options.C: Warmly decline and explain that reassurance feeds OCD
options.D: Tell her that the question itself is irrational

items.rationale: Reassurance is a compulsion. Declining warmly and explaining why supports recovery.

items.question: Hannah asks the counselor to accompany her to a restaurant for an exposure. What is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Go with her but leave it out of the clinical record
options.B: Plan it with informed consent and a documented rationale
options.C: Refuse, since out-of-office sessions are always unethical
options.D: Make it a social lunch to help her feel more relaxed

items.rationale: Out-of-office exposures can be appropriate when planned with informed consent and a documented rationale.

items.question: Which information BEST supports a personality disorder diagnosis rather than a mood episode?

options.A: Mood changes that happen within a single day
options.B: A history of self-harm during periods of distress
options.C: Having seen several therapists in the past
options.D: A pervasive pattern that began in adolescence

items.rationale: Personality disorders are pervasive, enduring patterns that begin by adolescence or early adulthood.

whyNot.A: Mood shifts occur in many conditions.

items.question: What is the FIRST clinical priority during intake?

options.A: Complete a personality inventory to confirm the diagnosis
options.B: Explore her family history and early attachments
options.C: Review what went wrong with her past therapists
options.D: Assess her current self-harm and suicide risk

items.rationale: Her self-harm history makes current safety the first priority.

items.question: Which treatment has the STRONGEST evidence for Alyssa's presentation?

options.A: Exposure and response prevention
options.B: Nondirective supportive therapy
options.C: Brief solution-focused therapy
options.D: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT)

items.rationale: Dialectical behavior therapy has the strongest evidence for BPD with self-harm.

whyNot.B: Lacks the structure BPD treatment needs.

items.question: What should the counselor do about contact between sessions?

options.A: Promise to answer any message as soon as possible
options.B: Decide how to handle contact case by case as it happens
options.C: Set a clear written policy on contact during informed consent
options.D: Refuse all contact of any kind outside of sessions

items.rationale: A clear written contact policy set during informed consent prevents misunderstanding.

whyNot.D: Too rigid; DBT includes structured coaching.

items.question: Alyssa arrives angry that the counselor didn't answer her texts. Which response is MOST validating?

options.A: “I'm not available on weekends, which we talked about when we started.”
options.B: “Let's talk about what really upset you about the breakup.”
options.C: “You were hurting and reached out, and my silence felt like being left.”
options.D: “Fourteen texts in one weekend is more than I can respond to.”

items.rationale: Validating her emotional experience, the hurt and the sense of being abandoned, de-escalates and repairs the rupture.

items.question: What is the purpose of DBT phone coaching?

options.A: A way to process trauma memories as they come up
options.B: An unlimited emotional support line for difficult moments
options.C: A replacement for weekly individual sessions
options.D: Brief help applying skills in the moment, within clear limits

items.rationale: DBT phone coaching is brief, skills-focused help in the moment, within clear limits.

items.question: The counselor feels drained and irritated. What is the BEST action?

options.A: Shorten her sessions to manage the counselor's energy
options.B: Transfer Alyssa to another counselor on the team
options.C: Bring it to consultation, such as the DBT consultation team
options.D: Tell Alyssa honestly that she is exhausting to work with

items.rationale: The DBT consultation team exists to support therapists and maintain treatment quality.

items.question: What is the main purpose of Alyssa's diary card?

options.A: To track urges, behaviors, and skill use
options.B: To give the counselor evidence of noncompliance
options.C: To replace verbal reports about her week
options.D: To teach her the habit of daily journaling

items.rationale: The diary card tracks urges, behaviors, and skill use to guide session priorities.

items.question: Which issue from the diary card should be addressed FIRST?

options.A: The missed work shift
options.B: Her urges to self-harm
options.C: Her feelings about the counselor
options.D: The fight with her sister

items.rationale: DBT's target hierarchy puts life-threatening behavior first, including urges to self-harm.

whyNot.C: Therapy-interfering issues come after life-threatening ones.

items.question: Which DBT skills module helps Alyssa get through a crisis without making it worse?

options.A: Walking the middle path
options.B: Distress tolerance
options.C: Interpersonal effectiveness
options.D: Emotion regulation

items.rationale: Distress tolerance skills help her survive a crisis without making it worse.

whyNot.A: Used in adolescent DBT, not crisis survival.

items.question: Alyssa says the counselor is the only one who really gets her. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Tell her that isn't true and that others understand her too
options.B: Acknowledge the connection and explore support outside therapy
options.C: Agree and encourage her to rely on sessions for support
options.D: Let the comment pass and return to the diary card

items.rationale: Acknowledging the connection while building outside support prevents over-reliance on therapy.

items.question: Alyssa asks to follow the counselor's personal Instagram. How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Block her account without explaining the reason
options.B: Discuss it openly, decline, and review the social media policy
options.C: Leave the question unanswered and move on
options.D: Accept the request, since the account is public anyway

items.rationale: Discussing it openly, declining, and reviewing the social media policy keeps the boundary clear and the alliance intact.

items.question: Which information BEST supports adjustment disorder rather than major depressive disorder?

options.A: He is worried about being a burden on his daughter
options.B: He is tearful and irritable with staff and other residents
options.C: He has no prior history of depression or anxiety
options.D: Onset within three months of a clear stressor, with no other disorder

items.rationale: Adjustment disorder starts within three months of a stressor and doesn't meet criteria for another disorder. He sleeps well, still enjoys baseball, and his symptoms began after the move.

whyNot.A: Burden worries occur in many conditions.
whyNot.C: A lack of history doesn't distinguish the two.

items.question: The staff counselor assumes Walter's sadness comes with his age. What does this reflect?

options.A: Cultural humility toward the older generation
options.B: Appropriate clinical judgment about older clients
options.C: An accurate view of emotional changes that come with late life
options.D: Ageist bias that could cause treatable distress to be missed

items.rationale: Assuming sadness is normal with age is ageism, and it risks missing treatable distress.

whyNot.C: Depression isn't a normal part of aging.

items.question: Given Walter's recent stroke, which additional screening is MOST important?

options.A: A substance use screen and nothing further
options.B: A career interest inventory to identify new activities
options.C: A personality inventory to understand his coping style
options.D: A brief cognitive screen such as the MoCA

items.rationale: After a stroke, a brief cognitive screen such as the MoCA is important.

items.question: Which approach is especially well suited to Walter?

options.A: Problem-solving therapy combined with life review
options.B: Long-term psychoanalysis
options.C: Exposure and response prevention
options.D: Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing

items.rationale: Problem-solving therapy and life review are effective for older adults adjusting to loss.

items.question: Walter asks, “At my age, what's the point?” What should the counselor do?

options.A: Reassure him that he has a lot to live for
options.B: Change the subject to his hobbies
options.C: Consider it a normal part of aging
options.D: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts

items.rationale: Hopeless statements in an older man with recent losses call for a direct suicide risk assessment.

items.question: Walter talks about missing his workshop and independence. Which response BEST reflects his experience?

options.A: “You've lost a lot that made you feel like yourself.”
options.B: “Maybe you can find a new hobby to replace it.”
options.C: “A lot of residents here feel the same way.”
options.D: “At least you're safe and cared for here.”

items.rationale: Reflecting his losses of identity and independence shows accurate empathy.

items.question: His daughter says he just needs to accept it. How should the counselor respond?

options.A: Explain the adjustment process and how to support his autonomy
options.B: Agree that acceptance is the goal of counseling
options.C: Exclude her from his care to protect his independence
options.D: Tell her that she's being unsupportive of her father

items.rationale: Psychoeducation about adjustment and supporting his autonomy helps the daughter support him.

items.question: What should the counselor do about Walter forgetting caregivers' names?

options.A: Diagnose a mild neurocognitive disorder
options.B: Screen his cognition and coordinate with his medical team
options.C: Assume it's a normal part of aging for someone who is 72
options.D: Ignore it, since he's still adjusting to the move

items.rationale: New forgetfulness after a stroke needs screening and medical coordination.

items.question: How should Walter's MoCA score of 23 be interpreted?

options.A: Possible impairment that needs further evaluation
options.B: Confirmation of a dementia diagnosis
options.C: Severe cognitive impairment
options.D: Normal cognitive functioning for his age

items.rationale: A MoCA score below 26 suggests possible impairment that needs further evaluation. It doesn't diagnose dementia.

items.question: Which goal BEST builds on Walter's progress?

options.A: Walter will accept that he can no longer drive himself
options.B: Walter will improve his relationships with staff and residents
options.C: Walter will stop feeling sad about the move
options.D: Attend the weekly VFW group at least three times in the next month

items.rationale: Specific, measurable, and built on his interest.

items.question: Walter plans to drive again against medical advice. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Report him to the state licensing agency
options.B: Tell him he isn't allowed to drive after his stroke
options.C: Explore what driving means to him and encourage a driving evaluation
options.D: Support his decision, since it's his right to choose

items.rationale: Exploring what driving means to him and encouraging a formal driving evaluation balances autonomy and safety.

items.question: The administrator wants details of Walter's sessions for a staff meeting. What should the counselor do?

options.A: Share the details, since staff need them to care for him
options.B: Refuse to share anything under any circumstances
options.C: Share everything, since the facility employs the counselor
options.D: Share only the minimum necessary, with Walter's consent

items.rationale: Share only the minimum necessary, with his consent.

whyNot.B: Some sharing may be appropriate with consent.
